newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Rains bring Philippine capital to a halt.
newsitem.headline: Rains bring Philippine capital to a halt.

text.p: Torrential rains brought Manila to a standstill on Tuesday, forcing government offices and financial markets to close for the day.
The downpour began on Monday evening and thousands of commuters were stranded in the capital after floods caused traffic jams, horrendous even by Manila's notorious standards.
"I was trapped on the expressway for nine hours last night," complained Ramon Lopez, a businessman who finally reached home in the suburbs at 1 a.m.
Commuters were ferried home in army trucks on Monday night and some families have had to be evacuated from low-lying areas, the National Disaster Control Coordinating Council said.
The weather bureau said the heavy rains were spawned by Typhoon Winnie which was heading towards China.
There were no immediate reports of any casualties, but strong winds disrupted power supplies in parts of the city.
Some international flights were delayed after crew members arrived late and at least 10 domestic flights were cancelled, the airport office said.
Government offices, banks and schools were closed for the day and the weather bureau predicted more rains for the rest of the day.
The rains brought a temporary respite to the country's beleaguered financial markets after their battering the previous day.

On Monday, the peso touched a record low over just over 30 to the dollar, a drop of about 14 percent since a wave of speculative attacks forced the central bank to allow a de facto devaluation on July 11.
Shares had also taken a hammering on Monday, with the composite index falling 3.28 percent to a 21-month low of 2,368.67.
Analysts said that the continued turmoil in Asia's currency markets would certainly keep both the peso and Philippine stocks under pressure.
Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the government was looking at possible measures to protect the peso from any further falls, though he declined to elaborate.
